title: scMAC: large language model-enhanced single-cell functional priors for completing functional context in bulk T cell receptor repertoires.
abstract: Bulk T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing enables scalable immune repertoire profiling but does not measure the transcriptional states required to infer T cell functional programs. Paired single-cell RNA/TCR sequencing offers a single-cell functional prior by jointly observing TCR identity and transcriptomic states. However, transferring this prior to bulk repertoires is challenging: sparse and noisy single-cell profiles can distort the functional reference, and the probabilistic relationship between TCR identity and transcriptome-inferred functional state makes direct cell-level alignment unstable, potentially biasing repertoire-level functional composition estimation. We present scMAC, a single-cell-guided framework for functional context completion that infers TCR functional representations reflecting transcriptome-derived T-cell states. scMAC builds a denoised functional reference by integrating multi-scale expression modeling with gene-semantic priors derived from large language model encodings of gene and protein descriptions, improving gene-level functional coherence. It then learns a prototype-guided TCR-to-function mapping that combines paired cell-level latent alignment with functional prototype regularization, enabling robust repertoire-level functional composition estimation. Across real single-cell and paired RNA/TCR datasets, scMAC outperformed existing single-cell representation methods in fine-grained cell-state representation, gene functional consistency, expression recovery, and disease-relevant pathway analysis, achieving an adjusted Rand index of 0.656 on a colorectal cancer dataset with 83 cell subtypes. For repertoire-level functional composition estimation, scMAC closely matched single-cell-derived functional proportions, with an R2 of 0.979 and a Bray-Curtis distance of 0.075. These results support scMAC as a practical route for transferring single-cell-derived functional knowledge to bulk TCR repertoire analysis beyond clonotype identity and clonal abundance. scMAC is publicly available at https://github.com/Bioinformatics7181/scMAC.

title: The Dosage Logic of PKD1: RNA Regulation and Therapeutic Derepression.
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is driven largely by heterozygous PKD1 mutations and insufficient functional polycystin-1 dosage, yet the mechanisms that regulate output from residual PKD1 alleles are only beginning to be defined. The PKD1 locus is unusually complex, and its transcript contains untranslated regions that actively constrain protein production. This review integrates genetic, molecular, and therapeutic evidence supporting a dosage-threshold model of cystogenesis. We discuss how gene architecture, RNA processing, and protein maturation set functional polycystin-1 levels, then focus on post-transcriptional control by the PKD1 5' and 3' untranslated regions. The 3'UTR contains conserved microRNA-binding sites, including a therapeutically actionable miR-17 site. Genetic disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of miR-17 increases polycystin dosage and attenuates cystic disease in experimental models. Farabursen, an anti-miR-17 oligonucleotide, has produced early clinical pharmacodynamic findings consistent with polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 derepression and is advancing into Phase 3 development. Together, these findings establish endogenous transcript derepression as a mutation-agnostic strategy for restoring gene dosage in ADPKD and provide a framework for treating other dosage-sensitive genetic disorders.

title: Molecular basis of DNA polymerase ζ's reverse transcriptase activity.
abstract: DNA polymerase ζ (Polζ) has emerged as a key reverse transcriptase in RNA-templated double-strand break repair (RT-DSBR), beyond its canonical role in translesion DNA synthesis (TLS). We present here the cryo-EM structure of yeast Polζ (including Rev1) in the act of reverse transcription, wherein the polymerase molds the replicative end of the bound RNA:DNA hybrid into B-like conformation and retains most contacts seen with DNA:DNA. Critically, the polymerase adopts the same conformation as with DNA:DNA, indicating its inherent versatility in accommodating both DNA:DNA and RNA:DNA substrates to preserve genome stability.

title: Regulatory Mechanisms of Alternative Polyadenylation in Plants: Roles of Poly(A) Protein Complexes in Transcriptome Plasticity.
abstract: Transcriptome plasticity is a key driver of proteome diversity, enabling organisms to finely tune gene expression in response to developmental cues and environmental stimuli, essential features for sessile plants facing constant challenges. Among the co-transcriptional processes contributing to this plasticity-such as alternative transcription start sites and alternative splicing-alternative polyadenylation (APA) plays a particularly prominent role, affecting 60%-70% of plant genes. Despite its prevalence, the molecular mechanisms guiding APA and its regulation remain incompletely understood. This review synthesizes recent advances in our understanding of how polyadenylation protein complexes-including Cleavage and Polyadenylation Specificity Factors (CPSF), Cleavage stimulation Factors (CstF), and Cleavage Factors (CF)-interact with cis-regulatory elements to determine poly(A) site choice. We highlight the coordinated actions of these protein families and their dynamic regulation across tissues, developmental stages, and environmental conditions. Furthermore, we propose a conceptual model of the regulatory network involving RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions that govern APA in plants. Deciphering these molecular networks offers promising avenues for targeted manipulation of APA to enhance crop resilience and productivity. Understanding the spatial and temporal regulation of polyadenylation machinery may ultimately enable precision control of gene expression in molecular breeding and agricultural biotechnology.

title: Isothermal Strand Displacement Amplification for Chemical Sensing: From Molecular Design to Integrated and Intelligent Platforms.
abstract: Strand displacement amplification (SDA) provides a versatile isothermal framework for chemical and biosensing, coupling polymerase-driven strand displacement with programmable nucleic-acid signal generation. Its analytical scope now extends beyond direct nucleic-acid detection because aptamers, DNAzymes, antibodies, and responsive probes can convert diverse recognition events into amplifiable DNA triggers. This review develops a unified view of SDA from molecular design to practical implementation, with particular emphasis on programmable amplicon generation, recognition-to-DNA transduction, interfacial confinement, cascaded amplification, and CRISPR coupling. The review follows SDA across biomedical, food, and environmental applications, including RNA biomarkers, liquid biopsy, genetic and epigenetic targets, proteins, enzymes, small molecules, and viruses. It also considers how these assays are being transferred into microfluidic, paper-based, lateral-flow, self-powered, regenerative, and intelligent systems. The important distinction is that analytical sensitivity does not necessarily predict practical performance. Extremely low detection limits often depend on cascaded processing beyond SDA itself, whereas real samples expose weaknesses in matrix tolerance, background suppression, reagent stability, fluid control, assay duration, and manufacturing reproducibility. Comparison with commercially established isothermal methods further shows that wider adoption will depend on converting flexible molecular chemistry into robust, standardized, sample-to-answer systems.

title: Creb1 aggravates glutamate-induced excitotoxicity and KA-induced seizure activity by transcriptionally activating Timp1.
abstract: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder, more common in children and the elderly. Although treatments have advanced, significant challenges remain. This study focuses on its molecular mechanisms to provide new insights and strategies for its treatment. Gene expression omnibus (GEO) database analysis, enrichment analysis, and the establishment of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were conducted for gene screening. HT-22 cells were treated with glutamate (Glu) to establish an in vitro epilepsy model. Gene knockdown and overexpression were achieved through cell transfection. Cell viability was measured by the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, while gene expression at the protein and messenger RNA (mRNA) levels was detected by western blot (WB) and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Flow cytometry was used to analyze apoptosis and mitochondrial membrane potential. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and Fe2+ levels were measured using commercial kits. Kainic acid (KA) was administered intraperitoneally to mice to establish an epilepsy animal model, which was used to verify the role of the gene in epilepsy development. Transcription factor binding sites in target gene promoters were predicted using the JASPAR database and validated by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and dual-luciferase reporter assays. Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 1 (Timp1) was highly expressed in tissue samples from the epilepsy mouse models of GSE88992 and GSE73878, as well as in the Glu-induced HT-22 cell model. In these models, Timp1 knockdown increased cell viability, reduced apoptosis, decreased LDH, promoted mitochondrial membrane potential, and lowered ROS, Fe2+, and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (Acsl4) levels. In KA-induced animal models, Timp1 knockdown reduced seizure score, cleaved caspase-3 (C-caspase3)/total caspase-3, and Acsl4 expression. cAMP response element-binding protein 1 (Creb1) transcriptionally activated Timp1. In the Glu-induced HT-22 cell model, Creb1 knockdown decreased Timp1 protein expression, increased cell viability and mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced apoptosis, LDH, ROS, Fe2+, and Acsl4 levels, while Timp1 overexpression partially reversed these effects. Taken together, Creb1 promotes the progression of epilepsy by activating Timp1, providing a new perspective and potential targets for epilepsy treatment. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01084-7.

title: RNASTOP: A Deep Learning Framework for mRNA Chemical Stability Prediction and Optimization.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines offer promising therapeutic potential for combating various diseases, yet their inherent chemical instability hampers long-term efficacy. Although several methods have been developed to predict mRNA degradation, they often suffer from limited accuracy and lack the capability for rational codon optimization. Here, we propose RNASTOP, a novel framework that integrates deep learning with heuristic search to simultaneously predict and optimize mRNA chemical stability. RNASTOP achieves a 13% improvement in accuracy over the top-performing model on the Stanford OpenVaccine competition dataset and demonstrates robust generalization in predicting full-length mRNA degradation. When applied to mRNA codon optimization, RNASTOP reduces the minimum free energy of the varicella-zoster virus vaccine sequence by 75.73% while maintaining high translation efficiency. Overall, RNASTOP serves as a powerful tool for predicting and optimizing mRNA chemical stability, accelerating the development of mRNA therapeutics. The source code of RNASTOP is available at https://github.com/xlab-BioAI/RNASTOP.

title: Considerations of Gene Expression Analysis Methods for Gapmer Antisense Oligonucleotide-Treated Samples.
abstract: Probe-based PCR assays are commonly used to evaluate gene expression in antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-treated samples, but assay design and postextraction processing may introduce substantial measurement bias. We investigated workflow-dependent differences in measured knockdown across PCR-based and RNA-sequencing assays using an allele-specific gapmer ASO, targeting a linked single nucleotide polymorphism of a dominant-negative SPTAN1 variant. Exogenous ribonuclease H (RNase H) activity during reverse transcription or ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-depletion inflated apparent knockdown and reduced RNA-sequencing coverage at the ASO-binding site. In droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), allele-specific detection probes overlapping the ASO-binding site produced substantially greater apparent knockdown than nonoverlapping probes, particularly following workflows with active RNase H. Spike-in experiments showed that this bias was not reproduced by adding ASO to purified RNA before complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis or to cDNA before ddPCR, but emerged when ASO was present during rRNA depletion. Together, these findings show that exogenous RNase H activity during RNA processing and ASO-probe overlap can distort measurements of gapmer-mediated transcript reduction. Poly(A)-based RNA sequencing, reverse transcriptase with reduced RNase H activity, and nonoverlapping PCR detection probes can minimize measurement bias when evaluating gapmer ASO-mediated knockdown.

title: HSV-1 ICP0 expression induces formation of nuclear TDP-43 assemblies.
abstract: Toxic cytoplasmic aggregates containing the nuclear RNA-binding protein TDP-43 form in several neurodegenerative diseases; however, the molecular triggers driving aggregation remain unclear. Epidemiological evidence has linked latent and reactivating herpes simplex virus type-1 (HSV-1) infections to neurodegenerative disease onset, but it is unknown if HSV-1 infection impacts TDP-43 subcellular distribution. Here, we demonstrate that HSV-1 infection of epithelial cells and DRG-derived neurons results in nuclear TDP-43 redistribution and TDP-43 accumulation within distinct nuclear assemblies. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 was not detected under these conditions. Nuclear TDP-43 assembly occurred early in infection and was dependent upon expression of the critical ICP0 regulatory gene. Remarkably, ectopic ICP0 expression in uninfected cells was sufficient for nuclear TDP-43 assembly. Thus, expression of a single viral gene product encoded by a near ubiquitous human herpesvirus can alter TDP-43 nuclear localization. Moreover, our work identifies a potential mechanistic link between herpesvirus infection and neuronal disease factor mislocalization.

title: Self-Monitoring Theranostic Nanomaterials for Biomedical Imaging and Cancer Therapy: Real-Time Visualization of Biodistribution, Payload Release, and Therapeutic Response.
abstract: Theranostic nanomedicines integrate therapeutic delivery with diagnostic imaging, but many conventional platforms primarily visualize nanocarrier localization and provide limited information on whether the therapeutic payload has been released, the intended treatment mechanism has been activated, or a meaningful biological response has occurred. Self-monitoring theranostic nanomedicines have emerged as functionally informative platforms capable of reporting their own biodistribution, biological fate, payload release, therapeutic activation, and downstream response in real time or through longitudinal imaging. This review summarizes the conceptual framework and design principles of self-monitoring nanomedicine, including always-on and activatable probes, Förster resonance energy transfer, self-quenching and dequenching mechanisms, ratiometric sensing, environment-responsive contrast agents, and multimodal imaging. Major imaging modalities, including fluorescence, magnetic resonance, photoacoustics, positron emission tomography, single-photon emission computed tomography, computed tomography, and ultrasound imaging, are discussed with emphasis on their respective capabilities and limitations for monitoring nanomedicine performance. Representative studies demonstrate the visualization of systemic biodistribution, target-site accumulation, carrier disassembly, drug and nucleic-acid release, photothermal and photodynamic activation, gene and RNA activity, oxidative stress, immune modulation, apoptosis, and pathogen clearance. Particular emphasis is placed on cancer theranostics, where self-monitoring nanomaterials can integrate tumor imaging with the assessment of intratumoral delivery, payload release, therapeutic activation, and early treatment response. Broader applications in inflammatory and immune-related diseases and infectious diseases further illustrate the general applicability of these monitoring principles beyond cancer. Despite substantial progress, clinical translation remains limited by ambiguous signal interpretation, insufficient quantitative validation, biological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and regulatory challenges. Future development should prioritize mechanistically defined and clinically actionable signals, orthogonal validation, standardized reporting, biodegradable and clearable materials, reproducible manufacturing, and compatibility with established imaging workflows. Self-monitoring theranostic nanomedicines may ultimately enable the transition from image-guided drug delivery to feedback-guided, adaptive, and personalized precision therapy.

title: Pulmonary Proteomic Responses to Subacute 2,2',5,5'-Tetrachlorobiphenyl-4-ol Exposure via a Subcutaneous Implant in Adolescent Female Rats.
abstract: Hydroxylated polychlorinated biphenyls (OH-PCBs) are biologically active metabolites that may contribute to adverse respiratory outcomes, yet their effects on the developing lung remain poorly characterized. This study investigated the impact of 2,2',5,5'-tetrachlorobiphenyl-4-ol (4-OH-PCB52), a human-relevant metabolite, on the pulmonary molecular pathways in postnatal day 28 female adolescent rats using a multi-omics approach. Animals were exposed to 4-OH-PCB52 (sham; low 1%; medium 5%; high 10%; (w/w)) via a subcutaneous implant release system for 28 days. Targeted analysis by gas chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (GC-MS/MS) detected 4-OH-PCB52 in the medium 5% and high 10% exposure dose groups. At both higher doses, proteomic profiling revealed significant alterations in protein markers related to pulmonary post-transcriptional regulation, metabolism and chemical biotransformation, immunity and inflammation, oxidative stress and programmed cell death, and surfactant production and mucociliary clearance. In contrast, RNA sequencing did not identify differentially expressed genes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that adolescent exposure to 4-OH-PCB52 perturbs key molecular markers associated with lung homeostasis, with potential implications for altered lung development and increased susceptibility to respiratory disorders during adulthood.

title: Integrated 13C Metabolic Flux and Multi-Omics Analyses Reveal Central Carbon and Redox Constraints in a Salt-Sensitive Chromochloris zofingiensis Mutant.
abstract: Saline cultivation can reduce freshwater demand and reshape the production physiology of high-value microalgae, yet the metabolic basis of strain-specific salinity tolerance remains unclear. Here, the astaxanthin-producing green microalga Chromochloris zofingiensis was examined by comparing the wild type (Cz-WT) with a cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG)-deficient mutant (Cz-pkg) under 100 mM NaCl. Physiological measurements were integrated with parallel 13C-glucose tracing, 13C metabolic flux analysis, LC-MS metabolomics, and time-series RNA sequencing. Relative to Cz-pkg, Cz-WT showed higher normalized fluxes from phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate and oxaloacetate, greater pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA conversion, and enhanced tricarboxylic acid (TCA)-cycle activity, suggesting a greater potential to support energy and reducing-equivalent metabolism. Cz-pkg exhibited lower glucose-6-phosphate and 6-phosphogluconate levels, early NADH depletion, and reduced pools of several amino-acid- and nucleotide-related metabolites. At 24 h, 141 genes were co-upregulated and 228 co-downregulated in both strains, involving photosynthetic electron transport, antioxidant metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, amino-acid metabolism, and terpenoid biosynthesis. Phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase was upregulated in both strains, supporting membrane-lipid remodeling. Overall, the data provide flux-level evidence that the salt-sensitive mutant is constrained in glycolysis-TCA cycle coupling and energy-redox homeostasis during salinity acclimation. Direct PKG substrates and causal phosphorylation events were not examined in this study.

title: 7α-Hydroxypaxilline, a Natural Product Isolated from Mangrove Endophytic Fungi, Inhibits Protein Translation in Vibrio alginolyticus.
abstract: Vibrio alginolyticus, a prevalent marine Gram-negative pathogenic bacterium, can cause vibriosis in aquaculture and pose potential threats to human health. The excessive abuse of antibiotics has aggravated the multidrug resistance of bacteria, driving researchers to explore natural antibacterial substances from mangrove endophytic fungi. In this study, four known indole-diterpenoids, 7α-hydroxypaxilline (1), paspaline (2), paspalinine (3), 4a-demethylpaspaline-4a-carboxylic acid (4), were isolated the marine-derived fungus Penicillium janthinellum D131. Among them, compound 1 exhibited superior inhibitory activity against Vibrio alginolyticus, with a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 0.781 μg/mL, which was superior to chloramphenicol (1.56 μg/mL). A series of phenotypic experiments confirmed the potent bactericidal activity of this compound. The results of multi-omics analysis and Western blot assays demonstrated that the compound disrupts the 50S ribosome-mediated translation process in bacteria. Molecular docking analysis and kinetic simulation were further performed to identify the target site, and the results revealed that the compound interacts with 23S ribosomal RNA (23S rRNA). In vitro translation assays further verified that the compound blocks bacterial protein synthesis by targeting 23S rRNA. This study reports the excellent anti-vibrio activity of 1, which is superior to chloramphenicol, and clarifies its ribosome-targeting mechanism of action. These findings provide a theoretical basis for the research and development of novel antibacterial drugs for aquaculture and broaden the potential applications of lead compounds.

title: Biological Complexity and Cryptographic Secrecy: Reproducible Key Recovery and a Structured Evidence Audit of Bio-Derived Key Schemes.
abstract: Bio-derived key schemes build cryptographic keys from biological material: protein structures, DNA and RNA sequences, amino-acid chains, proteinoid assemblies. This paper audits the class against a protocol drafted prospectively, refined during a pre-specified pilot, and frozen before the main screening and extraction, and tests its central claim empirically. No audited study reported a defensible attacker-conditioned min-entropy for its complete secret; the key-space figures instead measured an output or encoding-table size, a descriptor length, or a parameter-range product. A structured evidence audit of twelve studies finds that the biological material rarely holds the secret, that the evidence concerns the randomness of outputs rather than the secrecy of keys, and that no study provided a publicly linked runnable implementation. On three schemes (the two whose secret is a selection from a public set and one encoding scheme) we recover keys from the first two and bound the entropy of the third. The executed recoveries covered a 647-protein candidate set (work factor about 9.3 search-space bits) and a single-reference DNA position search (about 12 bits); a broader eight-reference analysis gives a projected search space upper bound of at most about 39 bits once a 16-bit auxiliary key is included, and was not exhaustively executed. Reported key spaces range up to millions of bits, and for the encoding scheme the input entropy is left unestablished. These results apply to schemes whose secret is public, a selection from public data, or an encoding; they do not extend to a scheme built on a genuinely private biological sample, a noisy physical measurement, or a properly constructed fuzzy extractor. We contribute a taxonomy of biological sources by role, three security observations, the audit and the recovery and accounting experiments, and a design checklist. Biological complexity does not by itself imply cryptographic secrecy.

title: Ire1-Mediated Unfolded Protein Response and Other Biological Phenomena in Ascomycota Yeasts and Filamentous Fungi.
abstract: Upon dysfunction of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), namely ER stress, eukaryotic cells commonly change their gene expression profile, resulting in enhanced ER functions. This cytoprotective response is called the unfolded protein response (UPR), whose molecular mechanism was first elucidated in pioneering studies using Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Ire1 is a transmembrane endoribonuclease that acts as an ER stress sensor. While Ire1-dependent unconventional splicing of mRNA encoding Hac1, the transcription factor responsible for UPR, was discovered in the 1990s, the precise mechanisms regulating their production and activation remain under investigation. Studies on Ire1 and Hac1 in other ascomycetes have also advanced, partly from the perspectives of clinical science and industrial applications, thereby uncovering some significant functional differences from those in S. cerevisiae. For instance, many ascomycete species other than S. cerevisiae likely perform regulated Ire1-dependent decay (RIDD), in which mRNAs encoding ER-client proteins are digested to mitigate ER stress. In certain species, Ire1 may preferentially shift its output toward HAC1 mRNA splicing or RIDD, depending on the type of stimulus. This review article provides an overview of classic and recent findings on the regulation and function of Ire1 and its target mRNAs in various ascomycete species.

title: Simufilam Regulates Mitochondrial Function in HEK293T TSC2 Knockout Cells.
abstract: The small molecule simufilam, also called PTI-125, has been reported to reduce cell overgrowth and seizure activity in a mouse model of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). TSC is a multisystem developmental disorder caused by mutations in TSC1 or TSC2, resulting in mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) hyperactivity and downstream cellular changes that contribute to focal malformations of the developing cortex and abnormal growth throughout the body. Here, to better understand the role of simufilam at the cellular level, we investigated the impact of simufilam on the proteome of TSC2 knockout (KO) HEK293T cells in vitro. We first validated that TSC2 KO cells displayed increased mTORC1 activity and elevated expression of the stress-associated marker ATF4 compared with TSC2 wild-type (WT) cells. Simufilam reduced ATF4 expression but did not attenuate mTORC1 activity. Next, using LC-MS/MS in TSC2 KO cells, we identified 514 differentially abundant proteins following simufilam treatment. Pathway and protein-protein interaction analyses revealed coordinated changes in mitochondrial translation and bioenergetic pathways, including mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and respiratory-chain-associated proteins, as well as pathways related to preribosome biogenesis, rRNA processing, RNA metabolism, and to some extent RHO GTPase-actin signaling, and chromatin/transcriptional regulation. Selected proteins from these pathways, including MRPS30, MRPL43, MRPL16, ALDH1L2, NDUFA6, and RBM19, were further examined by immunoblotting and found to be altered by simufilam treatment. Functionally, simufilam restored mitochondrial membrane potential in TSC2 KO cells. Overall, these findings support a potential mTORC1-independent role for simufilam in attenuating cellular stress and regulating mitochondrial function in TSC.

title: A σB-dependent sRNA provides a repressor function to the general stress response in Clostridioides difficile.
abstract: Clostridioides difficile is an anaerobic, gram-positive gastrointestinal pathogen that poses a significant health threat worldwide. A recent RIL-seq characterization of the Hfq-mediated RNA-RNA interactome revealed that small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators of virulence-related processes in C. difficile, including the initiation of sporulation. In the model Proteobacteria species E. coli and S. enterica, sRNAs often function as non-coding elements in vital stress responses mediated by alternative sigma factors, acting as repressors within these regulatory networks. However, whether this principle is broadly conserved across bacterial phyla remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that the Hfq-dependent sRNA SrsA is part of the regulatory network of the alternative sigma factor σB, which governs the general stress response in Firmicutes. Consequently, SrsA is highly expressed during the transition from exponential to stationary phase and under infection-related stress conditions, such as oxidative stress. We show that SrsA represses a highly conserved small protein family that regulates sporulation and three genes in the methyl-fixing branch of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP). Infection of mice further revealed that SrsA contributes to disease severity and bacterial recovery from antibiotic treatment in an acute and relapse mouse model of C. difficile infection. In summary, our data suggest that integrating SrsA into the σB regulon helps coordinate sporulation and vital metabolic pathways of C. difficile in response to infection-relevant stress conditions.IMPORTANCEThe central role of sRNAs as non-coding arms of stress responses represents a paradigm of sRNA function in Gammaproteobacteria. However, it remains unclear how broadly this regulatory principle is conserved across the bacterial tree of life. In our study, we identified the sRNA SrsA as a non-coding regulator involved in the sigma B-mediated stress response to nutrient limitation and radical stress in the intestinal pathogen Clostridioides difficile. We demonstrate that SrsA suppresses the production of a conserved family of spore regulators and of enzymes of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, establishing a role in regulating sporulation and gut colonization. Our work provides novel insights into the regulation of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, which is usually associated with autotrophic bacteria, and highlights the metabolic flexibility this anaerobic gut pathogen has evolved to survive in a nutrient-limited and inflamed gut environment.

title: Novel roles of the Epstein-Barr virus BRRF1 protein in post-transcriptional RNA regulation.
abstract: In lytic infection, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) proteins manipulate cellular processes in multiple ways to facilitate virion production and overcome host antiviral responses. Here, we screened a library of EBV lytic proteins for those that manipulate or localize to cellular processing bodies (PBs), known to play important roles in RNA surveillance and miRNA-mediated translational control. One EBV protein, BRRF1, was identified that partially localized to PBs, and affinity purification-mass spectrometry experiments showed that it interacted with the CCR4-NOT complex-a known component of PBs with multiple roles in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation. The CNOT9 subunit of CCR4-NOT was sufficient to bind BRRF1, and its downregulation diminished BRRF1 interaction with the CNOT1 scaffold protein, indicating its importance in mediating the CCR4-NOT interaction with BRRF1. A BRRF1 double-point mutant was generated that failed to bind CNOT9 or interact with CCR4-NOT and was used to assess the importance of the BRRF1-CCR4-NOT interaction. Luciferase reporter assays identified multiple roles for BRRF1 in post-transcriptional regulation, including polyadenylation-dependent destabilization effects and interference with miRNA function, the latter of which was dependent on BRRF1 binding to CCR4-NOT. In addition, mRNA sequencing experiments comparing cells with and without BRRF1 expression identified multiple transcripts affected by BRRF1, some of which were at least partly dependent on the BRRF1-CCR4-NOT interaction. These include Claudin 6, whose transcripts and protein were downregulated by BRRF1 expressed on its own, as well as in lytic infection. Thus, we have identified multiple roles for BRRF1 in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation, some of which involve interaction with CCR4-NOT. To efficiently generate virions, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) must manipulate cellular processes to optimize the environment and overcome host antiviral defenses. Through unbiased screening methods, we have identified an EBV protein (BRRF1) that localizes to cellular bodies, which play key roles in mRNA regulation, and that interacts with a cellular complex with multiple critical roles in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation. As expected from these interactions, we found that BRRF1 has multiple previously unknown roles in disrupting mRNA levels and translation. Interestingly, one of the transcripts targeted by BRRF1 is Claudin 6, which has multiple roles in cancers, leading to increased cell proliferation and invasion. Our study provides additional insight into how EBV proteins manipulate cells to promote infection and affect oncogenesis.

title: Hydrostatic Pressure-Mediated Chondrocyte Homeostasis in Osteoarthritis and Cartilage Engineering.
abstract: Articular cartilage homeostasis and osteoarthritis (OA) progression are strongly influenced by hydrostatic pressure (HP) within the joint mechanical microenvironment. Physiological-range HP (approximately 0.1-10 MPa in most experimental models) can maintain the chondrocyte phenotype, promote chondrogenic differentiation of stem/progenitor cells, support extracellular matrix (ECM) anabolism, and attenuate inflammatory, oxidative, and apoptotic signaling. By contrast, sustained or high-magnitude HP, particularly ≥20 MPa in injurious in vitro models, commonly shifts cartilage cells toward catabolism and cellular stress. Mechanistically, HP engages wingless-related integration site/β-catenin (Wnt/β-catenin), mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (MAPK/ERK), Hippo-Yes-associated protein (Hippo-YAP), noncoding RNA, epigenetic, heat-shock protein, and transient receptor potential (TRP) channel networks. Distinct from earlier reviews focused primarily on chondrogenesis or broad cartilage mechanobiology, this review integrates healthy and OA chondrocytes with progenitor-cell responses, compares HP delivery and culture systems, reconciles apparently contradictory parameter-response data, and evaluates translational opportunities and limitations. These comparisons support evidence-informed starting ranges for future HP protocols, while emphasizing that no single regimen is universally optimal.

title: Sacrificial Methionine Residues Protect Active-Site Histidines From Oxidation.
abstract: Histidine is the most common residue in enzymic active sites because of the chemical versatility of its imidazole side chain, but is also highly vulnerable to oxidative damage. Here, we demonstrate that methionine residues in secretory ribonucleases such as bovine RNase A serve as sacrificial antioxidants that protect active-site histidines. In the human homolog RNase 1, five methionine residues cluster near the catalytic histidines His12 and His119, which serve as a base and an acid, respectively, during RNA cleavage. Bioinformatic analyses reveal that these methionines are conserved across the RNase A superfamily and adopt S-aryl motifs with proximal aromatic residues that modulate the electron density at sulfur and thereby tune the susceptibility of methionine to oxidation. Chemoselective labeling of methionine with an oxaziridine probe increased the vulnerability of RNase 1 to oxidation-induced inactivation, implicating Met29 and Met35 as protective residues. Total chemical synthesis of an RNase 1 variant in which these residues were replaced by norleucine, a sulfur-free isostere of methionine, corroborated their protective role. A similar arrangement of methionines is present in unrelated secretory proteins, including serine proteases and calprotectin, suggesting a broadly recurring protective strategy.

title: Effects of transcription units and a specific hexanucleotide motif of porcine circovirus-like virus P1 on viral DNA synthesis, viral protein expression, and progeny virus production.
abstract: Porcine circovirus-like virus P1 has a broad host range and is known to cause post-weaning multisystemic wasting syndrome in pigs, as well as infect and propagate in cattle, goats, dogs, cats, yaks, and rabbits. To investigate the functional importance of its eight open reading frames (ORFs) and the conserved hexanucleotide motif (GGATCC), we generated a panel of site-directed mutants based on the P1 infectious clone rpSK-2P1. These mutants were transfected into PK-15 cells and serially passaged four times. Viral replication capacity and genetic stability were assessed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR), quantitative PCR, and Sanger sequencing. All the mutant viruses retained the ability to replicate their genomes and transcribe viral RNA. However, sequencing of viral genomes recovered at the fourth passage revealed selective reversion at multiple mutated sites, indicating a strong replicative advantage conferred by wild-type sequences during sustained propagation. Notably, mutant Y1, which harbored a mutation in ORF1 that encoded the capsid protein (Cap), initially exhibited reduced replication but rapidly reverted upon passaging, restoring Cap expression and fitness. These findings demonstrate that although these ORFs and nucleotide sites do not abolish P1 replication, their native sequences play pivotal roles in modulating replication efficiency and maintaining genetic stability, thereby providing key insights into the molecular mechanisms governing P1 replication. Thus, P1 tolerates limited genetic change but is under intense pressure to maintain its wild-type sequence, offering critical insight into the replication strategy and evolutionary constraints of this compact, broad-host-range DNA virus.

title: CircMED17 regulates bovine adipogenesis and fat deposition via mediating the proliferation and differentiation of bovine adipocytes.
abstract: Fat deposition is a key factor influencing beef quality. Therefore, understanding the regulatory mechanisms of adipogenesis is crucial for improving meat production traits in cattle. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as important post-transcriptional regulators in various biological processes, including adipocyte differentiation. In our study, circular RNA mediator complex subunit 17 (circMED17) was identified as a stable, nuclear-localized circRNA derived from exons 2 and 3 of the MED17 gene, with its expression markedly upregulated during bovine preadipocyte differentiation, suggesting its potential role in adipogenesis. Functional analyses revealed that circMED17 inhibits preadipocyte proliferation and apoptosis while promoting differentiation and lipid accumulation. Mechanistically, circMED17 exerts dual regulatory effects by sponging microRNA-146b (miR-146b) as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) and by directly interacting with the transcription factor GATA-binding protein 2 (GATA2). Importantly, the in vivo overexpression of circMED17 in obese mice increased subcutaneous fat deposition, confirming its pro-adipogenic role. Collectively, the findings reveal a previously unreported dual mechanism of circMED17 in bovine adipogenesis and highlight its potential as a molecular target for improving beef quality through genetic and breeding strategies.

title: Sense codon reassignment: from global proteome profiling to precision protein engineering.
abstract: The incorporation of non-canonical amino acids (ncAAs) has expanded the chemical diversity and functional repertoire of proteins beyond the 20 canonical amino acids (cAAs). While stop codon suppression introduces a single orthogonal decoding event, sense codon reassignment actively manipulates endogenous translational competition within the ribosomal decoding center. This strategy enables both proteome-wide stochastic labeling and precise site-specific modification of target proteins. In this review, we highlight recent advances in sense codon recoding strategies and their applications in nascent proteome profiling and precision protein engineering. We first discuss global metabolic labeling using endogenous aminoacyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetases and the programmable stochastic orthogonal recoding of translation (SORT) platform. We then examine site-specific approaches, including competitive rare codon recoding (RCR) in mammalian cells, genome-scale codon compression in Escherichia coli, and the creation of blank coding channels through total genome synthesis. These complementary paradigms have enabled high-resolution spatiotemporal mapping of nascent proteomes in live animals, multiplexed incorporation of up to five distinct ncAAs in a single mammalian protein, and the in vivobiosynthesis of complex sequence-defined polymers. By converting translational competition into an engineerable parameter, sense codon reassignment offers new opportunities to transform our ability to decode complex biological networks and develop next-generation molecular medicines.

title: Spinal Cord Stimulation Attenuates Cognitive Deficits in Chronic Pain in Association with Modulation of the Microglial lnc-PCM1/PCM1/PKC/IFN-γ Signaling Network.
abstract: Neuroinflammation plays a pivotal role in chronic pain with cognitive dysfunction (CPCD), a debilitating condition where effective treatments are limited. While spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established analgesic therapy, its potential to ameliorate cognitive deficits via central immunomodulation remains largely unexplored. A rat model of CPCD was generated by spared nerve injury (SNI). RNA sequencing was used to identify SCS-regulated long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in the prefrontal cortex (PFC). The functional involvement of the candidate microglial transcript NONRATT012007.2 (hereafter termed lnc-PCM1) was examined using adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated manipulation, behavioral testing, molecular assays, and primary-cell conditioned-medium experiments. SCS improved cognitive performance in CPCD rats. lnc-PCM1 was predominantly expressed in microglia and was reduced after SCS. Lower lnc-PCM1 expression was accompanied by increased pericentriolar material 1 (PCM1), reduced protein kinase C (PKC) phosphorylation and IFN-γ abundance, less M1-polarized microglial activation, and lower pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Conditioned medium from manipulated microglia produced corresponding changes in neuronal oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential, apoptosis-related proteins, and synaptic markers. In vivo overexpression of lnc-PCM1 or knockdown of PCM1 partially attenuated the cognitive and neuroinflammatory effects associated with SCS. The findings support an association between the cognitive effects of SCS and modulation of a microglial lnc-PCM1/PCM1/PKC/IFN-γ signaling network in the PFC. Because formal epistasis and IFN-γ neutralization or receptor-blockade experiments were not performed, the directionality and IFN-γ dependence of this network remain to be established.

title: Evaluation of Computational Neoantigen Prioritization Strategies for Personalized Cancer Vaccines.
abstract: Background: Identification of immunogenic neoantigens remains one of the major computational bottlenecks limiting the development of effective personalized cancer vaccines. Although various computational methods have been proposed for neoantigen discovery, there is little independent evidence regarding which approaches most effectively prioritize vaccine candidates using experimentally validated datasets. We focused on an independent multi-cohort benchmark of widely used neoantigen discovery pipelines and neoantigen scoring tools using publicly available datasets with experimentally validated immunogenic peptide-Major Histocompatibility complexes (MHC). Methods: In order to evaluate computational strategies used for selection of candidate vaccine peptides, five end-to-end neoantigen prediction pipelines and seven neoantigen scoring and prioritization tools were independently benchmarked using experimentally validated neoantigen datasets. End-to-end pipelines were evaluated on the TESLA cohort using raw WES and RNA-seq data from five patients, while individual prediction tools were additionally assessed on the TESLA, NCI, and HiTIDE validation cohorts comprising experimentally verified immunogenic and non-immunogenic peptide-MHC complexes. Results: NeoHunter achieved the highest overall recovery of experimentally validated neoantigens among the evaluated pipelines, while the scoring and prioritization tools NetMHCpan, MixMHCpred, and MHCFlurry generally showed the strongest ranking performance, although their relative performance varied substantially between datasets and patients. Precision-recall, average precision, and top K analyses demonstrated that no single predictor consistently dominated across cohorts and revealed a clear trade-off between candidate list size, precision, and recovery of validated neoantigens. Analysis of clinically relevant candidate selection thresholds demonstrated that restricting vaccine design to only the highest-ranked peptides substantially reduces sensitivity, whereas broader candidate selection improves recovery at the expense of increased experimental burden. Conclusions: These findings provide practical recommendations for computational selection of vaccine targets and highlight current limitations that must be addressed to improve the success of personalized neoantigen-based vaccines.

title: Single-Cell Whole-Transcriptome Detection Expands the Observable RNA Space for AI Virtual-Cell Models.
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has supplied cell atlases and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled virtual-cell models with scalable, gene-level descriptions of cellular state. Yet prevalent poly(A)-based counting assays capture only part of the RNA landscape. Here, "single-cell whole-transcriptome detection" denotes sequencing-based efforts to detect a broader range of RNA biotypes than conventional poly(A)-based gene counting; no assay detects or quantifies every cellular RNA species without bias. We compare RNA-capture scope, transcript-structure resolution, temporal labeling, spatial context, and additional modalities as distinct measurement dimensions. From a biosensing perspective, analytical sensitivity, transcript coverage, throughput, and assay bias determine which signals are available to computational models. We then examine cell-state representations, regulatory networks, dynamics, perturbation prediction, and foundation models. Total-RNA assays reveal additional non-coding RNAs, long-read methods inform transcript structure, and temporal assays constrain RNA kinetics. Whether these signals improve prediction beyond conventional gene-count inputs requires matched, task-specific model comparisons. We distinguish molecular observability, statistical association, predictive performance, and causal validation, which requires appropriate interventions. We propose benchmarks controlling sequencing depth, cost, model architecture, and held-out samples while testing feature ablations, out-of-distribution performance, uncertainty calibration, and experimental outcomes. Together, high-throughput poly(A)-based profiling and broader RNA measurements provide complementary cellular breadth and regulatory depth.

title: Dengue virus-2 triggers Epstein-Barr virus replication in primary B cells by co-opting the IRE1-XBP1 signaling axis.
abstract: The intricate interplay between co-infecting viral pathogens within a host can significantly influence disease outcomes. Dengue virus (DENV), a globally prevalent arbovirus from the Flaviviridae family, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a ubiquitous human herpesvirus, share extensive geographical overlap, yet their potential interactions remain largely uncharacterized. This study elucidates a novel molecular mechanism whereby DENV-2 infection triggers disruption of EBV latency. We systematically demonstrate that DENV-2 infection consistently induces EBV lytic gene expression and viral replication in diverse cellular contexts, including epithelial cell lines and, critically, in primary human B lymphocytes-the principal reservoir of latent EBV. Mechanistically, we establish that the substantial burden of DENV-2 protein synthesis and replication induces profound endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, activating the unfolded protein response (UPR). Through pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockdown, we dissect the three UPR branches and identify the IRE1-XBP1 signaling axis as the indispensable pathway for this phenomenon. DENV-2 infection promotes the endoribonuclease activity of IRE1, leading to the unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA into its transcriptionally active isoform, XBP1s. Depletion of IRE1 or XBP1 attenuated DENV-induced BZLF1 expression, whereas ectopic XBP1s expression increased BZLF1 transcription. Our findings delineate a precise virus-host-virus signaling model in which an acute RNA virus engages a cellular stress pathway to promote entry into the EBV lytic program and viral genome amplification. This provides a new paradigm for understanding the pathobiology of dengue fever and the complex dynamics of the human virome.IMPORTANCEThis research uncovers a previously unrecognized molecular dialog between two of the world's most common viral pathogens. By demonstrating that dengue virus infection can awaken dormant Epstein-Barr virus, this study provides a mechanistic basis for the long-suspected but poorly understood complications arising from viral co-infections. We pinpoint a specific cellular stress pathway, the IRE1-XBP1 axis of the unfolded protein response (UPR), as the critical molecular switch. This discovery is significant because it not only explains how an acute viral illness can trigger the reactivation of a latent, potentially oncogenic virus but also opens new avenues for therapeutic intervention. Understanding this intricate interplay could lead to novel strategies for managing severe dengue and other diseases where viral co-infection is a contributing factor to pathogenesis.

title: Blood transcriptomic signatures of vascular risk in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Lifestyle and environmental factors contributing to cardiovascular risk are components of the exposome, yet molecular signatures associated with cumulative cardiovascular risk in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain incompletely understood. We analyzed blood-based transcriptomics data from two independent cohorts: Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH; N = 148, Korean) and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; N = 743, predominantly European ancestry). Framingham cardiovascular risk score (FRS)-associated co-expression network modules were identified, followed by pathway-based enrichment, hub gene-based participant stratification, and bidirectional cross-cohort discovery-replication analyses. Two co-expression modules were associated with FRS in SNUBH, and six in ADNI. Bidirectional analyses identified two preserved modules with consistent module-FRS associations across cohorts, enriched in pathways implicated in cellular responses to exposure, including RNA-protein homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and hematopoietic processes. Hub genes in the two modules stratified participants into molecularly distinct subgroups concordant with clinical FRS categories. FRS-associated molecular pathways were identified and warrant further investigation as potential targets for risk modification.

title: Efficient permuted intron-exon RNA circularization system based on the LtrB group II Intron from Lactococcus lactis
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as promising platforms for stable RNA expression and therapeutic applications, but methods for their generation remain limited. Here, we engineered the Lactococcus lactis LtrB group II intron into a permuted intron-exon (PIE) configuration to enable efficient circRNA formation (circLtrB). Among the tested split designs, LtrB domain IV cleavage yielded the highest circularization efficiency. Although LtrB encodes LtrA maturase required for efficient in vivo splicing, in vitro application of LtrA to the PIE constructs resulted in lower circularization efficiency than self-splicing conditions. We further examined circularization under distinct salt conditions and showed that NH4Cl- and KCl-based splicing buffers independently support high circularization efficiencies (>80%), while producing distinct splicing intermediates, indicating ion-specific mechanistic effects on circularization. Extending outer homology arms did not enhance circularization efficiency, demonstrating that efficient circRNA formation in the circLtrB platform is independent of extended exon pairing interactions. Using this system, we generated circRNAs across a range of coding sequence lengths, highlighting its payload flexibility. To optimize translation, we evaluated multiple internal ribosome entry sites (IRES), including Aichivirus, Crohivirus, CVB3, improved EMCV, HRV, and Salivirus, and found that the CVB3 IRES drove the highest translation efficiency. Linear NLuc showed faster decay kinetics, while circLtrB-NLuc exhibited more sustained expression over time. Transcriptome-wide RNA sequencing revealed comparable innate immune responses between circular and linear RNAs. Together, these results establish circLtrB as a versatile and efficient platform for circRNA production, providing mechanistic insight into group II intron-mediated circularization and expanding the toolkit for functional circRNA engineering.

title: Tumor-suppressive tRNA-derived RNA fragment itRF-GlnCTG targets the RBMX-m6A axis to destabilize RCN1 mRNA in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tsRNAs) have been recognized as important regulators in human cancers. However, the role of tumor-suppressive tsRNAs in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) has not been thoroughly characterized. This study sought to elucidate the function of tsRNA-Gln-i-0061 (itRF-GlnCTG) in ESCC and its underlying molecular mechanism. Bioinformatic approaches were employed to characterize the expression profile of tsRNAs in ESCC. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and in situ hybridization (ISH) was applied to validate its expression levels in clinical samples. Functional assays, including proliferation and migration experiments, were conducted to detect the function of itRF-GlnCTG in ESCC. To identify downstream targets, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), biotin pull-down and mass spectrometry were performed. Additionally, the interaction between itRF-GlnCTG, the m6A reader RBMX, and reticulocalbin-1 (RCN1) mRNA was examined to uncover the regulatory mechanism. We identified itRF-GlnCTG as a downregulated tsRNA in ESCC tissues, and its elevated expression level correlated with better patient outcomes. Functionally, itRF-GlnCTG inhibited the growth, motility, and adhesion capabilities of ESCC cells. Mechanistically, itRF-GlnCTG acted as a molecular decoy by competitively binding to the m6A reader protein RBMX. This interaction impaired RBMX's SUMOylation, sequestered it in the cytoplasm, and thereby disrupted RBMX-mediated, m6A-dependent stabilization of RCN1 mRNA, leading to suppressed RCN1 expression. The combination of serum itRF-GlnCTG with CEA and CA199 showed high diagnostic efficacy for ESCC (AUC = 0.94). Our results uncover a novel tumor-suppressive function of itRF-GlnCTG in ESCC by targeting the RBMX-m6A axis to destabilize oncogenic RCN1 mRNA. This study underscores the diagnostic utility of itRF-GlnCTG and reveals a new tsRNA-m6A regulatory pathway in ESCC.

title: Physiological and Transcriptional Responses of the Blood Clam Anadara kagoshimensis (Tokunaga, 1906) During Cadmium Exposure.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) exposure can affect metal handling, metabolism and tissue condition in bivalves on different timescales. We examined these responses in the blood clam Anadara kagoshimensis (Tokunaga, 1906) exposed to a nominal Cd concentration of 100 μg/L. Respiration, tissue Cd, redox biomarkers and histology were assessed over 480 h, alongside hepatopancreas RNA profiles at 0 h, 24 h and 21 d. Oxygen consumption reached its lowest exposed mean at 96 h. At 480 h, Cd concentrations were 44.23 ± 8.99 μg/g dry weight in the hepatopancreas and 31.75 ± 1.81 μg/g in the gill. SOD and CAT activities followed tissue-specific trajectories, GSH content declined, and MDA showed non-monotonic changes. Histological observations included epithelial detachment and disruption of digestive tubule structure. Descriptive expression comparisons identified metal handling, redox, cell-death and immune-related candidates, with more twofold expression differences at 21 d than at 24 h. qRT-PCR examined ten selected targets using three tank-derived RNA samples per time. Together, the physiological measurements, tissue observations and exploratory expression profiles describe a tissue- and time-dependent response to Cd exposure and identify candidates for further functional study.

title: Gene Expression Dynamics in Monilinia fructicola and Prunus persica During the Battle for Infection Revealed by Dual RNA-Seq Analysis.
abstract: Brown rot, caused by Monilinia fructicola, poses a significant threat to global peach production, but the molecular interactions underlying host defence and pathogen colonisation remain incompletely defined. In this study, we used dual RNA-Seq to simultaneously capture the gene expression profiles of Prunus persica and M. fructicola during early infection (12 and 24 h post-inoculation). High-depth sequencing enabled a detailed analysis of transcriptional dynamics in both organisms. P. persica displayed a delayed yet robust defence response with marked activation of immune signalling, oxidative burst, cell wall fortification, hormone signalling, and secondary metabolism at 24 hpi. M. fructicola initiated infection rapidly, first expressing cell wall-degrading enzymes, then upregulating protein synthesis, energy metabolism, effector proteins, phytotoxins, and stress adaptation genes. Integrated analysis revealed a tightly coordinated interplay between fungal virulence strategies and peach defence mechanisms, including cell wall modification and immune responses. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for host-pathogen dynamics, offering actionable insights for developing resistant peach cultivars for field cultivation and for targeted strategies to improve post-harvest disease management and fruit shelf-life.

title: A Telomere-to-Telomere Genome Assembly and Demographic History Inference of Ostrya rehderiana.
abstract: Ostrya rehderiana is a critically endangered plant species with an extremely small population size. However, the absence of high-quality genome assembly has impeded the understanding of the causes and genetic consequences of its endangered status, especially how theses genetic consequences result in the failure of its population regeneration. In this study, we integrated PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore (ONT) long-read sequencing, Hi-C, Illumina resequencing, and RNA-seq data to generate a telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly and annotation for this species. The assembled genome has a total size of 349.04 Mb and was successfully anchored to eight pseudochromosomes. A total of 28,698 protein-coding genes were predicted, of which 27,476 were functionally annotated. The BUSCO completeness score reached 98.9%, indicating a high level of assembly completeness and accuracy. Based on this T2T genome assembly, we reconstructed historical changes in effective population size using the PSMC model. The results revealed pronounced long-term fluctuations in population size, followed by a recent continuous decline. This study provides an important genomic resource for exploring the mechanisms underlying the endangered status of O. rehderiana offering a foundation for conservation genetics research on plant species with extremely small populations.

title: Spatially dissecting drivers of inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity in Kenyan breast cancer.
abstract: Despite growing evidence on the impact of intra-tumoral heterogeneity (ITH) in breast cancer (BC), its biological drivers and clinically relevant mitigation strategies remain poorly characterized, particularly in low-resource settings where spatial profiling is rarely applied. To address this gap, we conducted a comprehensive, multiplatform spatial profiling study of BC in a Kenyan population. Using the NanoString GeoMx™ Digital Spatial Profiler, we quantified 44 protein markers across 707 spatially defined, PanCK-segmented Areas of Illumination (AOIs) from 31 tumors. All tumors exhibited measurable ITH, with one-third showing marked heterogeneity. Sixteen patients exhibited two or more intrinsic subtypes within their tumors, three of whom had three subtypes. Immune-related ITH was particularly pronounced for CD8 and CD68. AOI phenotype (epithelium- vs. stroma-rich) emerged as the primary driver of marker variability. Linear mixed-effects (LME) modeling further revealed that intrinsic subtype influenced not only classical subtyping markers (ER, PR, HER2) but also immune and signaling markers including IDO1, S100B, PTEN, and BCL-2. Tissue morphology and spatial neighborhood contributed additional variance, particularly in stroma-rich AOIs, while incorporating AOI spatial coordinates improved model fit and revealed further spatially structured heterogeneity. Nonetheless, over 25% residual variability remained for most markers, suggesting unmeasured biological or microenvironmental influences. Comparisons with InSituPlex and bulk RNA data demonstrated that bulk profiling could obscure or misrepresent tumor complexity, underscoring the need for integrative spatial approaches. Our findings highlight whole-slide, multi-region digital profiling as a practical and scalable strategy to capture clinically relevant heterogeneity in low-resource settings.

title: Gut microbiota-derived ornithine aggravates hypofibrinogenemia induced by tigecycline via disturbing fibrinogen mRNA stability.
abstract: Tigecycline has been regarded as the last resort strategy for complex infections caused by multidrug-resistant pathogens. Nonetheless, due to hypofibrinogenemia its clinical use may have to be suspended. However, the mechanisms of hypofibrinogenemia induced by tigecycline are still unknown. In this study, untargeted metabolomics were conducted in a prospective patient cohort by using feces samples from patients with and without hypofibrinogenemia following tigecycline administration. We found a significant difference in fecal metabolic profile between patients with and without hypofibrinogenemia, especially ornithine. Transferring gut microbiota from subjects with hypofibrinogenemia induced ornithine accumulation and exhibited coagulation dysfunction in the recipient mice. Next, we demonstrated that co-treatment with ornithine and tigecycline upregulated the m6A modification, accelerated cell senescence, and decreased the mRNA stability of FGA and FGB, thereby reducing fibrinogen levels in HepG2 cells. Interestingly, knockdown of methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3) increased fibrinogen levels by enhancing the stability of mRNAs associated with fibrinogen synthesis, whereas overexpression of METTL3 showed the reverse effects. Notably, YTH N6-methyladenosine RNA binding protein 2 (YTHDF2) was involved in the regulation of FGA and FGB mRNA stability in the METTL3-mediated m6A modification process. The results of animal experiments also verified that excessive ornithine could aggravate tigecycline-induced fibrinogen reduction and decrease blood coagulation activity in a METTL3-dependent manner. Collectively, our study demonstrated that gut microbiota-derived ornithine aggravates hypofibrinogenemia induced by tigecycline via regulation fibrinogen mRNA stability. Our study provides novel insights and preventive therapeutic strategies against tigecycline-induced hypofibrinogenemia.

title: Accelerated Senescence of Fibroblast-Like Cells Derived from Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells of a Patient with Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch Progeroid Syndrome.
abstract: The study of senescence dynamics in cells obtained from patients with accelerated aging syndromes provides a model for understanding the fundamental mechanisms of cellular senescence and for the search for approaches to slowing it down. Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch progeroid syndrome, caused by a mutation in the gene encoding the catalytic subunit of RNA polymerase III POLR3A, is a poorly studied syndrome with the earliest manifestation of accelerated aging features. Previously, we obtained induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from the fibroblasts of a patient with this syndrome. These iPSCs displayed changes in nucleolar structure, genome instability, and impairments in telomere maintenance mechanisms, as a result of which the telomeres did not elongate during reprogramming of the patient's fibroblasts into iPSCs. During iPSC differentiation, we obtained fibroblast-like cells (secondary fibroblasts), which were used to study dynamics of accelerated senescence. Expression of the mutant POLR3A was decreased in the secondary fibroblasts compared with the iPSCs; however, features of accelerated senescence were already detectable at early passages, manifested as increased β-galactosidase activity and increased expression of the cell-cycle inhibitor p16. Differentiation was accompanied by a pronounced shortening of telomere length, which had not been restored during the reprogramming of the patient's cells into iPSCs. The data obtained demonstrate that genomic instability of stem cells exerts an accelerating effect on the development of progeroid features during cellular differentiation.

title: RNF152 inhibits immune evasion in clear cell renal cell carcinoma by promoting the ubiquitination of PD-L1.
abstract: Dysregulation of ubiquitination drives tumor progression in various cancers, including clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). RING finger protein 152 (RNF152) is a ubiquitin E3 ligase that regulates cancer development. This study aimed to investigate the role of RNF152 in ccRCC and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanism. RNF152 expression and its correlation with survival were analyzed through bioinformatics analysis of the RNA expression profile from TCGA. Tumor cell viability and colony formation, as well as cytotoxicity of co-cultured CD8+ T cells, were assessed. Tumor growth and immune evasion were evaluated using a tumor-bearing mouse model. Furthermore, whether RNF152 regulates PD-L1 via ubiquitination was investigated. RNF152 was expressed at low levels in ccRCC, and high RNF152 expression correlated with better patient survival. Overexpression of RNF152 inhibited proliferation and immune evasion of ccRCC cells in vitro, while knockdown of RNF152 had the opposite effects. Moreover, RNF152 promoted degradation of PD-L1 by facilitating K48-linked polyubiquitination, and the ubiquitination site was identified as K64. Additionally, overexpression of PD-L1 counteracted the inhibition of proliferation and immune evasion induced by RNF152. In vivo, anti-PD-L1 therapy inhibited tumor growth and immune evasion in mice with RNF152 knockdown. facilitating ubiquitination of PD-L1. These findings reveal a novel regulatory mechanism in ccRCC and highlight the therapeutic potential of upregulating RNF152 to enhance anti-tumor immunity, potentially in combination with anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy.

title: The stability explanation for lncRNA discovery bias is not testable with current half-life coverage.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are nominated as candidate disease regulators from steady-state RNA-seq differential-expression (DE) catalogs, and short-lived lncRNAs have been proposed to be systematically missed because rapid decay lowers steady-state abundance. We asked how much of that bias it can account for, using 18 half-life strata drawn from 16 metabolic-labeling datasets across 13 human cell lines and 17 uniformly processed disease cohorts (16 TCGA tumor-versus-normal contrasts, one non-alcoholic fatty liver cohort; recount3), matching the half-life cell line to the tumor tissue where possible. Under the pre-filter used here the abundance floor leaves only 24% of annotated lncRNAs testable, and downsampling BRCA recovers just 18% of its full-cohort DE lncRNAs at n = 5 per group. Its upstream driver is not resolved. Across six tissue-matched half-life datasets - four cell lines - the median half-life-abundance correlation is ρ = 0.195 (cluster-bootstrap range - 0.003 to 0.293, descriptive rather than a formal interval at so few clusters); dropping the weakest match gives 0.143. Among the lncRNAs carrying a half-life we find no excess exclusion of the short-lived relative to the long-lived; but half-lives are measurable only where a transcript is expressed, and only in cell lines, so that comparison is confined to a subset selected on the quantity at issue. The limiting factor is coverage: only 10.0% of annotated lncRNAs, and 4.4% of those below the filter, have any measured half-life - under 1% counting tissue-matched cell lines only. We provide SIEVE, open-source code producing these detectability figures for a given design, and specify the data the hypothesis needs.

title: Genetic Insights into the Comorbidity of Congenital Heart Disease and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Focus on Copy Number Variations.
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) and neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) frequently co-occur, indicating that cardiac and neural phenotypes can arise from shared developmental disturbances rather than exclusively from the physiological consequences of heart disease. Copy number variations (CNVs) provide a major genomic basis for this overlap, but their effects extend beyond changes in protein-coding gene dosage. This review synthesizes evidence from recurrent CNV syndromes, genomic cohorts, developmental studies, and experimental models to define how CNVs jointly influence heart and brain development. We examine four interconnected mechanisms: dosage alteration of pleiotropic and multiple genes, disruption of non-coding regulatory elements, remodeling of non-coding RNA networks, and reorganization of three-dimensional chromatin architecture. We further describe how developmental timing, cell-type-specific regulatory context, additional genomic variants, cardiac physiology, and clinical exposures shape incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. Together, these findings support a layered model in which a primary CNV establishes cross-organ susceptibility, whereas genetic and developmental modifiers determine whether CHD, NDD, or both become clinically manifest. Clinically, CNV diagnosis can inform neurodevelopmental surveillance, multisystem management, and genetic counseling. Genotype-first longitudinal cohorts, developmental multi-omics, parallel cardiac and neural models, and prospective clinical studies will advance individualized risk prediction and intervention.

title: Single-cell analysis of 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD)-treated murine skin demonstrates that sebaceous gland differentiation precedes Ahr-dependent seboatrophy, with elevated expression of infundibular Blimp1.
abstract: In humans, 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) induces chloracne, a skin condition that presents with acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, sebaceous gland (SG) atrophy (seboatrophy), and hamartomas. Although chloracne-like phenotypes have been reported in TCDD-treated mice, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Previous studies showed that TCDD-induced CYP1A1 protein is expressed in LRIG1+ progenitor cells in hair follicles, suggesting that TCDD targets specific cell populations within the pilosebaceous unit. To explore the effects of TCDD on the epidermis and pilosebaceous unit, we analyzed single-cell RNA expression in wild-type and Ahr-null mice at postnatal day 21 (P21) following in utero and lactational exposure. The results showed that TCDD preferentially induced the AHR target genes Cyp1a1 and Cyp1b1 in the lower infundibulum and subjacent junctional zone overlapping the LRIG1+ progenitor cell niche. TCDD also caused Ahr-dependent seboatrophy, accompanied by increased expression of Blimp1, a transcriptional repressor that regulates SG size. A second site of Cyp1a1 induction was the SG, where Cyp1a1 was markedly elevated in the basal proliferating cells and immature sebocytes. In a 3-day topical exposure study of early effects, TCDD produced a dose-dependent increase of Cyp1a1 expression in the SG that included the more differentiated sebocytes. This response was accompanied by expansion of the Scd1-positive area, elevated Nile Red lipid staining, and an increased number of Blimp1-high sebocytes, demonstrating that TCDD enhanced SG differentiation and lipid production in vivo. These changes preceded the onset of Ahr-dependent seboatrophy, providing new insight into the cellular and molecular events underlying chloracne pathogenesis.

title: Full-length transcriptome analysis reveals candidate genes involved in phenylpropanoid pathway in Euphorbia maculata.
abstract: Euphorbia maculata is a herbaceous plant in China, known for its medicinal properties. The main active components of E. maculata are flavonoids. However, the biosynthesis mechanism of flavonoids in E. maculata remains poorly understood due to the limited availability of genetic information. In order to explore the flavonoid biosynthesis mechanism of this species, we carried our study. A total of 20,238 non-redundant transcript isoforms were acquired with an N50 length of 2,994 bp and an average length of 2,766.82 bp. Of these isoforms, 20,069 (99.16%) were successfully annotated in NR, Swissprot, KOG, GO, and KEGG databases. Additionally, 20,085 coding sequences (CDSs), 117 long noncoding RNAs (LncRNAs), and 971 transcription factors (TFs) were identified from the full-length transcriptome data. The RNA-Seq data was then analyzed using the full-length transcriptome as a reference sequence, revealing 27 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) involved in phenylpropanoid pathway in E. maculata. These included 15 PAL, 5 C4H, 4 4CL, and 3 CHS genes. The expression levels of these DEGs were found to vary in the leaf and stem across five different periods, with the majority of phenylpropanoid pathway genes being upregulated in the stem compared to the leaf at the same period. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis revealed that the bHLH, HD-ZIP, bZIP, MYB, FAR1, and AP2 may regulate the expression of 5 C4H and 3 CHS. Furthermore, through analyzing the correlation between the expression levels of DEGs and the accumulation of flavonoids in various tissues of E. maculata at different stages, we found that 2 PAL, 2 C4H, 1 4CL, and 2 CHS may play a crucial role in regulating flavonoid biosynthesis in this species. Our study enriched the genomic resources and revealed candidate genes involved in phenylpropanoid pathway in E. maculata. These findings provide candidate gene resources for further investigation of the flavonoid biosynthesis mechanism in E. maculata.

title: Nuclear respiratory factor 1 supports NPM1 expression and contributes to the regulation of a subset of ribosome biogenesis genes.
abstract: Nucleolar proteins support ribosome biogenesis in proliferating cells, but their expression levels have not been systematically compared with those of ribosomal proteins. We analyzed Human Protein Atlas RNA-sequencing data from 1132 cancer cell lines, comparing 280 ribosome biogenesis-related genes with 88 ribosomal protein (RP) genes. RP genes were generally highly expressed, whereas expression of ribosome biogenesis-related genes varied widely. NPM1 was the most highly expressed gene in the latter group, with expression comparable to that of many RP genes. To investigate how NPM1 expression is maintained, we analyzed its promoter using reporter assays and identified a proximal sequence that supports promoter activity. A dominant-negative nuclear respiratory factor 1 (NRF1) mutant reduced reporter activity when its putative target sequence was present. NRF1 knockdown decreased endogenous NPM1 mRNA level, and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) detected NRF1 at the proximal NPM1 promoter. Analysis of public NRF1 ChIP-sequence data revealed promoter-proximal occupancy at a subset of ribosome biogenesis-related genes, including NPM1, FBL, and DKC1. NRF1 binding to the FBL and DKC1 promoters was also confirmed by ChIP assay, and expression of both genes decreased upon NRF1 knockdown. These findings identify NRF1 as a contributor to the expression of a subset of ribosome biogenesis-related genes.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Proteomic Analyses Reveal Wheat Responses Associated with High-Temperature All-Stage Resistance to Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici.
abstract: The obligate biotrophic fungus Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst) frequently overcomes host immunity through rapid evolution. The wheat landrace Paozimai exhibits high-temperature all-stage resistance (HTAS) to Pst, a type of resistance expressed at relatively high temperatures across all growth stages. In this study, we investigated host-pathogen interactions using integrated transcriptomic and data-independent acquisition proteomic analyses. Dual RNA-seq analysis at 192 and 216 h post-inoculation (hpi) revealed a shift in enriched Pst pathways during the late latent period, from endoplasmic reticulum protein processing and fatty acid metabolism at 192 hpi to carbohydrate and glutathione metabolism at 216 hpi. In the host, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were enriched in defense-related signaling pathways at 192 hpi and in metabolic pathways at 216 hpi. Co-expression network analysis identified ribosomal and protein biosynthesis processes that may contribute to defense. Proteomic analysis showed greater overlap across time points, with oxidative phosphorylation enriched at 192 hpi and glycan biosynthesis at 216 hpi. Furthermore, integrated multi-omics and co-expression network analysis identified 16 candidate wheat genes, including genes encoding ribosomal proteins and stress-response proteins. These findings describe temperature-associated host and pathogen responses during HTAS and nominate candidates for functional validation.

title: Physiological Responses and Time-Course Transcriptomic Analysis of Morchella sextelata Strain Mel-21 During NaCl Exposure.
abstract: Salt stress limits fungal growth and distribution, but the mechanisms underlying salt tolerance in Morchella remain unclear. Here, we combined physiological measurements, transcriptomic analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and heterologous expression assays to characterize salt-stress responses in Morchella sextelata.
